summary: Describes how a BGP router can check whether the Autonomous System originating a route is actually authorized by the holder of that address prefix. It relies on validated RPKI data and helps reduce accidental or malicious route hijacks, though it only partly addresses the wider problem of BGP security.

eli5.summary: Imagine someone claims to be the mail carrier for your street. This is a way for the post office to check a list and see whether that person is really allowed to deliver there.

subtitle: How a BGP router checks that the network announcing an address block is really allowed to originate it.

tldr.problem: BGP routers believe whatever origin an announcement claims, so a network can announce address space it does not hold, by mistake or on purpose.
tldr.mechanism: The router compares each route's prefix and origin AS against a local table of Validated ROA Payloads taken from the RPKI, and labels the route Valid, Invalid or NotFound.
tldr.outcome: Operators can filter or de-prefer Invalid routes through policy. It checks only the origin, not the path, so the RFC calls it more a protection against misconfiguration than strong security.

facts.label: VRP contents
facts.value: IP address, prefix length, maximum length, origin AS number

facts.label: Scope
facts.value: Origin AS only, no path validation

today: RFC 6811 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 8481 and RFC 8893; it has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Checking Who Originates a Route
sections.content:
A BGP route ties an address prefix to the list of Autonomous Systems (ASes) the announcement has passed through, carried in the AS_PATH attribute. The list starts with the AS that originated the prefix. RFC 6811 addresses one security requirement: validating that the AS claiming to originate a prefix is in fact authorized by the prefix holder to do so.

The RFC says plainly that this is only a partial answer. Checking the whole path of a route is outside its scope. What it defines is a simple mechanism by which a BGP speaker assigns a validation state to each prefix in a received BGP UPDATE message.

The data comes from the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI), where Route Origin Authorizations (ROAs) are signed objects that link ASes to blocks of IP addresses. A relying party fetches a local copy, checks the signatures and keeps it refreshed. How the router gets that data is out of scope here; the RFC points to RFC 6810. It also notes that any other database mapping prefixes to authorized origin ASes could be used.
sections.eli5: Anyone can shout that they own a house on your street. This idea keeps an official list of who really owns which house, so you can check before you believe them.

sections.title: Validated Payloads, Covered and Matched
sections.content:
The BGP speaker loads validated objects from the cache into local storage. Each holds an IP address, a prefix length, a maximum length and an origin AS number, and is called a Validated ROA Payload (VRP).

Two relations between a route and a VRP drive everything:

  • Covered: the VRP prefix length is less than or equal to the route prefix length, and the two addresses are identical for all bits the VRP prefix length specifies. In other words the route prefix is the VRP prefix or more specific than it.
  • Matched: the route prefix is Covered by the VRP, the route prefix length is no more than the VRP maximum length, and the Route Origin ASN equals the VRP ASN.

The Route Origin ASN is the rightmost AS in the final AS_SEQUENCE segment of the AS_PATH. If the final segment is AS_CONFED_SEQUENCE or AS_CONFED_SET, or the path is empty, it is the speaker's own AS number. For any other final segment type it is the special value NONE, which no VRP can carry, so such a route can never be Matched.
sections.eli5: A VRP is one line in the list: "this street, this many houses, this owner." A claim is covered if it falls inside that street, and matched if the claimant is also the listed owner.

sections.title: The Three Validation States
sections.content:
Given those definitions, every route lands in exactly one state:

  • NotFound: no VRP Covers the route prefix.
  • Valid: at least one VRP Matches the route prefix.
  • Invalid: at least one VRP Covers the route prefix, but none Matches it.

The order in which VRPs are visited does not matter, because the resulting state is fully determined. An AS number of zero is never valid for a route, so no route is Matched by a VRP whose ASN is zero. The RFC includes pseudo-code that loops over the covering entries and returns Valid on the first match; where it disagrees with the prose, the prose is authoritative.

A BGP speaker SHOULD run this lookup for each route in a received UPDATE, and SHOULD apply it to routes redistributed into BGP too. If validation is not performed on a route, its state SHOULD be initialized to NotFound.
sections.eli5: There are three answers. "Not on the list at all", "on the list and the right owner", or "that street is on the list but this is the wrong owner".

sections.title: Policy Control and the Local Cache
sections.content:
An implementation MUST let operators match and set the validation state in its route policy filtering. It MUST also support four-octet AS numbers, as in RFC 6793. The state is treated as a local property of the route, not a new BGP attribute. An implementation MUST NOT drop a route from the Adj-RIB-In or from the decision process because of its validation state unless explicitly configured to.

Each speaker is expected to talk to one or more RPKI caches. Prefix-to-AS mappings change over time, so when a mapping is added or deleted the implementation MUST re-validate any affected prefix and run the BGP decision process if needed.
sections.eli5: The router keeps its own sticky note on each route saying what it found. It only throws a route away if the grown-ups (the operators) told it to.

sections.title: What Operators Do With the State
sections.content:
Once a route has a state, policy decides what to do. The RFC lists two ideas: filter routes by state, for example rejecting all Invalid routes, or change preference by state, for example by adjusting LOCAL_PREF. Considering Invalid routes in the decision process is a purely local policy matter and should be done with utmost care.

Sometimes a policy changes a property that is not propagated into Internal BGP (IBGP). Then it can be needed for routing correctness to pass the validation state to IBGP peers. The RFC suggests setting a community or extended community on the sending side, and matching it and setting the state on the receiving side.
sections.eli5: After checking, the router can ignore suspicious deliveries or just trust them a little less. How strict to be is up to each network.

sections.title: Limits of the Protection
sections.content:
The scheme is only as good as the database behind it. If Invalid routes are blocked, an attacker who can inject or remove records in the validation database could make an otherwise valid route look Invalid, which is a possible denial-of-service vector.

The protection is also limited against a determined attacker: they need only prepend the valid source AS to a forged announcement to defeat the check. The mechanism does not protect against AS-in-the-middle attacks and does no path validation. The authors conclude that it should be thought of more as a protection against misconfiguration than as true security in the strong sense.

The RFC also notes the RPKI is loosely consistent, like the DNS, so one cache or router may hold different data about a prefix than another. It says there is no fix for that.
sections.eli5: The list can be tampered with, and a clever cheat can still pretend to be the right owner. So it mostly catches honest mistakes.
